title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
Cline, an AI coding tool, deployed an autonomous agent to respond to GitHub issues with overly broad permissions and no validation of its inputs. An attacker could use prompt injection to make the agent execute arbitrary code, then steal the credentials it used to publish updates to package registries. This is a model deployed to make decisions about system access without the human review that would have caught the injection vulnerability.

The agent operated from late December 2025 through February 9, 2026, when the vulnerability was disclosed and fixed within one hour. The researcher who discovered it reported it through official channels starting January 1 but received no response, then went public. It is not established whether anyone successfully exploited the vulnerability before it was patched, though the reporting suggests an attempt may have been made.

summary:
Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability from late December 2025 through February 9, 2026. The tool's developers added an AI agent to automatically respond to GitHub issues, but this agent was configured with overly broad permissions and could be manipulated through prompt injection attacks. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that an attacker could craft a malicious issue title to trick the AI into running arbitrary code, then use a technique called cache poisoning to steal publishing credentials. These credentials would have allowed someone to release malicious updates to Cline across the Visual Studio Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM package registry, potentially compromising millions of developers' computers.

Khan attempted to report the vulnerability through official channels starting January 1, 2026, but received no response despite multiple contact attempts. After going public with the disclosure on February 9, Cline fixed the vulnerability within one hour by removing the AI workflow and making other security improvements. Khan's evidence suggests someone may have already attempted to exploit the vulnerability, though no malicious updates were published. Cline advised users to disable auto-updates until the company could confirm no one had stolen production credentials.
